newsitem.title: USA: Columbia moves to placate feds, but worries investors.
newsitem.headline: Columbia moves to placate feds, but worries investors.

text.p: Moving decisively to blunt a massive federal probe of its business, Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. announced a sweeping reorganization Thursday that may appease Washington at the price of aggravating Wall Street.

The largest U.S. for-profit hospital company said it will sell or spin off its fast-growing home health division, directly addressing a key target of the investigation that has plunged the Nashville, Tenn.-based company into crisis.
The move to jettison home health may remove a legal irritant, but industry analysts said it could also hurt the future of a $20-billion company famous for its relentless expansion.
"What we're going to see is a much slower-growth company, much less aggressive," said Robert Gold, a health care analyst at Standard & Poor's Equity Group in New York.

Confronting allegations of improper Medicare billing, Columbia said it will widen disclosure of its Medicare cost reports, impose a new review system on Medicare coding procedures and adopt a new regulatory compliance programme.

Annual cash incentive pay for employees will be ended. "Eliminating short-term cash incentive compensation will simply remove any appearance of pay being tied to short-term objectives," said Dr. Thomas Frist, the company's newly appointed chairman and chief executive.
Columbia employs 285,000 people. Upper management will be hit hardest by the cash incentives halt, the company said.

The company also reiterated that it will halt a controversial practice of selling interests in hospitals to physicians. "Such interests unintentionally may lead to the appearance of conflicts of interest," i said in a statement.
Existing syndication arrangements involving physician ownership in Columbia hospitals will be dismantled where possible, the company said.
In addition, Columbia said it will change its laboratory billing procedures, another area under investigation, and set stronger guidelines on transactions with physicians.

The wide-ranging package of reforms fulfils a pledge made last week by Frist, 58, to have a clear plan before federal authorities as soon as possible following his July 25 appointment as successor to former CEO Richard Scott.
"We have already committed to cooperating with all governmental agencies, but we need to do more," Frist said in a statement outlining his reform plans.

A four-month old investigation of Columbia by several federal agencies led last month to raids on 33 company facilities in six states and seizures of cartloads of files pertaining to laboratory billing and home health care.

Three Columbia midlevel managers were indicted last week on fraud charges. Shareholders have filed at least 11 lawsuits against the firm and the attorneys general of Florida, Texas and Alabama are investigating the company.

Columbia's former CEO and its president were ousted on July 24 by the board of directors. Frist, formerly vice chairman, replaced Scott. On Monday, Jack Bovender, 51, a close friend and former subordinate of Frist, replaced former President David Vandewater.
Frist and his father cofounded Hospital Corp. of America, or HCA, in 1968. Three years ago, HCA was acquired by Columbia, which Scott started with financial partners in 1987.

Columbia said it hired the Washington, D.C. law firm of Latham & Watkins and the Big Six accounting firm of Deloitte & Touche, giving both broad powers to examine company practices, recommend new policies and procedures and work with the government.

Columbia's core business consists of 342 acute-care hospitals. Its home health business, assembled in recent years from various acquisitions, generated about 5 percent of 1996 revenues totalling nearly $20 billion, the company said.

While that may appear to be a small slice of total sales, analysts said it is a vital component because it subsidises some of Columbia's less-profitable acute-care hospitals. Stripped of that support, some small-market hospitals may flounder, they said.
Columbia said it hopes to sell or spin off the home health unit but maintain a means of deriving revenue from the business.
"What we would like to do is find a strategic partner or strategic partners ... to make sure that we don't lose this continuum of care," Bovender said.
The company's stock fell 37.5 cents to close at $34 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.
